articles.title: Bihar Plans 500 MW Rooftop Solar For Govt Buildings Under RESCO Model
articles.description: The Bihar Renewable Energy Development Agency (BREDA) has initiated a tender process to empanel solar power developers for setting up 500 MW of grid-connected rooftop solar projects on government buildings across the state under the Renewable Energy Service Company (RESCO) model. Under the tender, selected Solar Power Developers (SPDs) will be responsible for the design, engineering, supply, installation, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of the rooftop solar plants, according to a tender extension notice issued by BREDA. The tender has been floated now which seeks empanelment of SPDs for the 500 MW programme. No Proposed Tariff The RESCO structure is expected to enable solar deployment on government buildings without requiring the government building owner to undertake the complete upfront project development and operational responsibilities. However, the tender extension notice does not specify the proposed tariff, project-wise capacity allocation, contract tenure, financing structure or payment mechanism. BREDA has revised the tender schedule, with online sale of the tender document beginning from September 10, 2026. The pre-bid meeting is scheduled for September 18 at 2:30 pm at BREDA's office in Patna. Submission Dates Interested bidders can submit their tender documents online until 2 pm on October 5, 2026. Physical submission of the original EMD, tender document cost, bid processing fee and the required undertaking relating to non-blacklisting or debarment will be accepted until 2:30 pm on the same day. The techno-commercial bids are scheduled to be opened from 3:30 pm on October 5, while the date for opening of financial bids will be communicated separately to eligible bidders through email. The proposed 500 MW programme could create a sizeable distributed solar pipeline across Bihar's government-building estate, while shifting project development, installation and long-term O&M responsibilities to empanelled private developers through the RESCO route. However, details on the number and type of government buildings to be covered, individual rooftop capacities, expected generation, tariff discovery and the duration of the RESCO agreements are not provided in the tender extension notice and would need to be examined in the detailed RFP documents. Similar Tales From Other States Bihar's 500 MW programme comes amid a wider expansion of RESCO-based rooftop solar procurement for government buildings. In Uttar Pradesh, UPNEDA issued a tender in April 2025 for 500 MW of grid-connected rooftop solar PV projects on government and semi-government buildings and other institutions, with projects to be implemented under the RESCO model through tariff-based competitive bidding. The UP programme allowed capacities ranging from 1 kWp to 2 MWp and provided for net-metering or net-billing arrangements. Delhi has also pursued the model through IPGCL, which floated a 50 MW government-building rooftop solar programme divided into 25 packages of 2 MW each under RESCO. More recently, Tamil Nadu has moved to select developers for 20 MW of rooftop solar projects on government buildings under RESCO through tariff-based competitive bidding. The model is also being used at the central level. In 2026, SECI invited bids for 12.25 MW of rooftop solar projects on Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya buildings under RESCO through tenure-based competitive bidding, while REIL has issued a tender for 15 MW of solar projects on government buildings across different states and Union Territories under the same model

articles.title: CM Omar bets on film industry to create jobs for Kashmir youth
articles.description: Srinagar , Sep 10: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Thursday said the ongoing International Film Festival J&K (IFFJK) in Kashmir could open a new avenue of employment for local youth saying the government was working to equip young people with skills required by the film industry. Talking to reporters at Gupkar, CM Omar said efforts were being made to train local youth in areas such as camera work and film production so that they could secure opportunities in the growing industry. “You will definitely get a chance, but a new series of employment can start here,” he said. The CM said that the government was, from the first day of the festival, looking at ways to help local youth enter the film industry. He said that local youngsters would be encouraged to undertake courses in camera work, production and other technical aspects of filmmaking, enabling them to get opportunities to work in the sector. On a protest by a Kashmiri Pandit seeking accommodation, CM Omar questioned the basis of the demand, saying that accommodation had already been allotted to those eligible. “Which Kashmiri Pandit is without accommodation? Not one of them is homeless,” he said. The CM said the administration was ready to address the issue if anyone genuinely required accommodation, but criticised that people have a tendency to protest without sufficient reason. “This has become a tradition to protest for no reason,” he said. CM Omar said anyone still requiring accommodation should approach the administration, saying that those eligible had been allotted accommodation. On the controversy surrounding the playing of the full stanzas of Vande Mataram at official functions, he said the administration was bound by statutory obligations and that the requirement applied across the country, not merely in Jammu and Kashmir. The CM said official functions featuring the national anthem would also include the national song as required under the applicable law, arguing that the issue should not be turned into a controversy. “We have never accepted Vande Mataram as a party. We will not accept it in the future either. But we will have to fulfil our legal and statutory obligations,” he said. CM Omar also defended National Conference chief spokesman TanvirSadiq over remarks concerning the historical poverty of Kashmiris, saying the issue was documented by historians including Walter Lawrence. He said Kashmir witnessed a period of severe poverty when people were trapped under the influence of landlords and other intermediaries, and "referring to that history did not warrant an apology." “This is a historical fact. But Kashmir has since progressed to a stage where families were educating their children and producing doctors and engineers," the CM said. "Neither Tanvir nor any other party member needs to tender apology for what Tanvir said on poverty in Kashmir." He also accused the BJP and PDP of having a “common issue” and playing together on the controversy. On the upcoming BRICS summit in Delhi, CM Omar said the government’s functioning would not be affected, saying that the Cabinet meets every month and that the government’s agenda could not be halted.

articles.title: Two-day Vendor Development Programme Jointly organised by CMPDI and MSME-Development Office, Ranchi concludes successfully
articles.description: 10 September 2026: Central Mine Planning and Design Institute, a Mini-Ratna subsidiary of Coal India Limited and MSME-Development Office, Ranchi; Ministry of MSME, Government of India jointly organised a two-day Vendor Development Programme-cum-Product Exhibition - 2026 at Ranchi on 9 th and 10 th September, 2026. The programme was jointly inaugurated on 9th September, 2026 by Chairman of the programme, Shri Chaudhari Shivraj Singh, CMD, CMPDI, along with the Chief Guest, Shri Nilendu Kumar Singh, CMD, CCL, and other dignitaries. Speaking on the occasion, Chaudhari Shivraj Singh, CMD, CMPDI emphasized that the Vendor Development Programme is not merely a buyer-seller meet, but a platform to foster long-term partnerships between corporates and MSMEs. Singh stressed on the significant role of MSMEs in promoting indigenisation, innovation and specialised solutions, and aligning their expertise with the requirements of corporates/PSUs can create new avenues of growth towards Viksit Bharat. Highlighting CMPDI’s diverse range of services, from exploration and geomatics to environmental services and mine closure, Shri Singh urged MSMEs to leverage these opportunities and their specialised capabilities to grow from local entities into globally competitive enterprises. Chief Guest Nilendu Kumar Singh, CMD, CCL, in his address, said that micro and small enterprises can play a vital role in building an Atmanirbhar Bharat and assured them of all possible support. He urged all participants to make the best use of the programme and develop their products and enterprises in accordance with the changing needs of the time. Indrajit Yadav, Director, MSME-Development Office, Ranchi, briefed the participants about the objectives and outline of the programme. He stated that the programme would provide micro and small entrepreneurs an opportunity to interact directly with the officials of the public sector undertakings participating in the event. Pankaj Kumar, Chief Vigilance Officer, CCL & CMPDI, stated that the Vendor Development Programme, being organised under the Vigilance Awareness Campaign 2026, would promote transparency and fairness in the government procurement process. Nripendra Nath, Director (T/CRD), CMPDI, said the programme provides a platform for MSMEs to interact with buyers/Corporates, understand their requirements. He particularly encouraged women entrepreneurs to actively participate and leverage these opportunities for business growth. During the First Day’s ‘Technical sessions and Buyer-Seller Meet’, senior officials from CMPDI, CCL, BSL/SAIL, Bokaro, Hindustan Copper Limited, South Eastern Railway, GAIL and NTPC Mining Limited, GeM provided detailed information regarding their respective procurement and vendor registration processes on GeM (Government e-Marketplace), briefed the participants in detail about TReDS (Trade Receivables Discounting System). On the second day of the programme, during the Buyer-Seller Interaction Session and Technical Session, officials from CMPDI, UCIL, SIDBI and MECON Limited, Ranchi provided information on the procurement processes for products/services required by their respective organisations under the Public Procurement Policy. Representatives of NSSH/NSIC, Ranchi, and the MSME Development Office, Ranchi, elaborated on various schemes of the Central and State Governments for General, Women and SC/ST MSME entrepreneurs. A total of five (05) public sector/government organisations and 15 micro and small enterprise units displayed their products through exhibition stalls at the programme. More than 200 MSME entrepreneurs participated in the technical sessions and directly interacted with officials during the question-and-answer session to seek clarification on their queries.

articles.title: BRICS Summit 2026 in New Delhi: 15 Big Themes That Could Reshape Trade, MSMEs and the Global South
articles.description: India prepares to host the 18th BRICS Summit as an expanded 11-member grouping looks beyond geopolitics towards trade, MSME finance, innovation, digital infrastructure, sustainable development and stronger Global South cooperation When leaders of the BRICS nations assemble at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on September 12–13, 2026, the significance of the meeting will extend far beyond another gathering of major emerging economies. For India, the 18th BRICS Summit represents an opportunity to demonstrate whether an enlarged BRICS can evolve from a high-level geopolitical forum into an increasingly practical economic cooperation platform capable of creating opportunities for businesses, MSMEs , exporters, startups and investors. India is hosting the summit during its fourth BRICS Chairship, having earlier chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The year is also significant because 2026 marks 20 years since BRICS began its journey. The summit will bring together leaders of BRICS member and partner countries as well as outreach invitees. According to the Government of India, more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements across over 25 Indian cities have preceded the leaders' meeting, spanning political and security cooperation, economic and financial engagement and people-to-people exchanges. BRICS itself is considerably different from the grouping India chaired five years ago. It now consists of 11 members — Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE , Saudi Arabia and Indonesia . Collectively, these economies represent around 49.5 per cent of the world's population, approximately 40 per cent of global GDP and around 26 per cent of global trade , according to Indian government estimates. For SMEStreet, the critical question therefore is not simply what political declaration will emerge from New Delhi. The bigger question is: Can India help turn the economic scale of BRICS into measurable opportunities for entrepreneurs and businesses? Here are the 15 major themes to watch . 1. New Delhi Could Mark the Beginning of a More Implementation-Oriented BRICS India's overarching theme for its 2026 Chairship is “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability” , deliberately forming the BRICS acronym. The formulation is important because it shifts the conversation from institutional expansion towards economic delivery. India's official approach has also been described as people-centric and rooted in the philosophy of “Humanity First.” The government says its 2026 engagements have emphasised practical and development-oriented outcomes rather than diplomacy alone. This distinction matters. After a period of major expansion, BRICS faces a natural next-stage challenge: demonstrating that the larger grouping can convert political influence into workable economic mechanisms. New Delhi could therefore become less about who joins BRICS next and more about what existing BRICS members can actually build together. For businesses, measurable progress could include easier financing, digital trade infrastructure, market-access platforms, standards cooperation, technology partnerships and stronger development financing. The success of the summit should ultimately be measured not merely by the length of its declaration but by the number of initiatives that progress from discussion to implementation. 2. India Will Seek to Strengthen its Leadership of the Global South The New Delhi summit gives India another platform to position itself as a bridge between advanced economies and emerging markets. BRICS today covers economies from Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East, giving the grouping a geographic and economic reach that was unimaginable when Brazil, Russia, India and China began formal coordination two decades ago. India's challenge will be to ensure that enlargement does not dilute the developmental agenda. Issues such as access to finance, technology, resilient infrastructure, affordable energy, food security, healthcare, entrepreneurship and digital inclusion are particularly important for developing countries. Consequently, India's leadership opportunity lies in ensuring that BRICS does not become defined simply by geopolitical opposition to other international blocs. A more economically credible BRICS would instead complement existing institutions while seeking reforms that provide emerging economies with a stronger voice. For India, this fits into a broader diplomatic approach of strategic autonomy: engaging multiple global groupings while maintaining independent relationships across competing geopolitical camps. 3. Global Governance Reform Will Remain a Central Political Theme One of BRICS' longest-standing arguments is that international governance structures should better reflect changes in the global economy. Emerging economies today account for a considerably larger proportion of world output and consumption than when many multilateral institutions were designed. That makes reforms in global financial governance, multilateral decision-making and international institutions an important continuing BRICS 2026 agenda. The discussion has economic implications. Representation in international financial institutions influences development finance, sovereign borrowing, infrastructure funding, financial stability and rule-making. For countries across the Global South, reform therefore goes beyond diplomatic prestige. The New Delhi summit provides India with an opportunity to advocate reform while simultaneously emphasising that existing multilateral institutions and rules-based mechanisms must remain functional. That balance will be important because BRICS members themselves possess different economic systems, strategic priorities and relationships with Western institutions. Consensus, rather than ideological uniformity, remains BRICS' most realistic operating model. 4. The USD 1.17 Trillion Intra-BRICS Trade Opportunity Could Move Centre Stage Trade is likely to emerge as one of the most economically important subjects surrounding the summit. India's Commerce Ministry says intra-BRICS merchandise trade increased from approximately USD 84 billion in 2003 to USD 1.17 trillion in 2024 , representing a thirteen-fold expansion. But this figure simultaneously demonstrates how much opportunity remains untapped. The expanded BRICS now connects enormous consumer markets, commodity producers, manufacturing hubs, energy exporters, technology ecosystems and rapidly growing middle-class populations. India has advocated balanced and expanding intra-BRICS trade, stronger services trade and more resilient and diversified global value chains . These principles were reflected in the BRICS Trade Ministers' Meeting held in Jaipur in August 2026. For Indian exporters, the commercial opportunity extends well beyond conventional merchandise. Potential growth sectors include pharmaceuticals, healthcare, engineering goods, automobile components, food processing, textiles, IT services, fintech, digital services, renewable-energy equipment, electronics, machinery, professional services and education. A structured BRICS business ecosystem could help companies view the bloc not simply as eleven separate markets but potentially as an interconnected opportunity network. 5. MSME Finance Could Become One of India's Most Important BRICS Legacies For SMEStreet's MSME audience, one development deserves particularly close attention. At the August 2026 BRICS Trade Ministers' Meeting, members agreed upon the Jaipur Consensus and guiding principles relating to MSME credit. Among the initiatives is the examination of a possible BRICS invoice-discounting mechanism , alongside credit-assessment guiding principles for export-oriented MSMEs. This could eventually become extremely significant. One of the biggest barriers faced by small exporters is not necessarily lack of demand. It is the gap between receiving an order and receiving payment. Businesses frequently need working capital for manufacturing, inventory, logistics, compliance, insurance and salaries while waiting weeks or months for invoices to be settled. Invoice discounting allows companies to raise financing against receivables rather than waiting for final payment. If BRICS countries can eventually develop interoperable frameworks around invoice financing, export-credit assessment or fintech-enabled trade finance, thousands of smaller companies could potentially participate in international trade. India's MSME Ministry had already made access to finance a core theme of the first BRICS SME Working Group meeting in April, including fintech-enabled SME lending and seamless global trade payments. The summit should therefore be watched carefully for political endorsement of these mechanisms. 6. The First BRICS MSME Forum Signals a Shift Towards Small Businesses Another important development of India's Chairship has been the hosting of the first BRICS MSME Forum in Agra in June 2026. The event brought policymakers, government representatives, business leaders and entrepreneurs together to discuss stronger MSME ecosystems across BRICS countries. This institutionalisation is important. Historically, international economic platforms have frequently been dominated by large companies and government institutions. But MSMEs generate employment, regional economic activity, entrepreneurship and export diversification across developing economies. Creating a dedicated BRICS MSME architecture could allow cooperation around financing, digitisation, technology adoption, skills, sustainability, market access and cross-border partnerships. For India, this presents an opportunity to take platforms developed domestically for MSME formalisation, digital payments, e-commerce and digital credit and use them as reference models for wider Global South collaboration. The longer-term possibility should be the emergence of a genuine BRICS MSME marketplace where businesses can discover suppliers, distributors, technology partners, financiers and customers across member economies. 7. A Common BRICS Trade Platform Could Transform Buyer-Seller Connectivity An especially significant proposal surfaced just days before the summit. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal called for stronger work towards a common BRICS trade platform and greater connectivity between businesses across participating economies. Such an initiative could have major long-term consequences if converted into a practical digital platform. Imagine an Indian engineering MSME being able to discover procurement requirements from Brazil, an Indian food processor identifying distributors in the UAE or Saudi Arabia, or an African enterprise sourcing technology services from India through a recognised BRICS business environment. The concept could potentially bring together buyers, sellers, trade-finance institutions, export-promotion organisations and business chambers. However, technology alone would not guarantee success. For such a marketplace to become commercially useful, BRICS countries would need to address authentication of businesses, payment protection, dispute resolution, logistics, standards, documentation, language barriers and data interoperability. If those challenges can be addressed, a BRICS business platform could become one of the grouping's most visible benefits for smaller companies. 8. Women-Led Enterprises Could Gain a Larger International Market Women's entrepreneurship has been another significant element of India's Chairship. BRICS discussions during 2026 covered women's digital and financial inclusion, entrepreneurship, leadership, skills and participation in economic development. Immediately before the summit, Piyush Goyal urged BRICS partners to expand access to credit, exhibitions, buyer-seller meetings and international markets for women-owned enterprises and called for progress towards making the proposed Women's Advancement Fund a concrete initiative. This is potentially more consequential than a traditional gender-development initiative. Women-owned MSMEs frequently face a combination of financing constraints, smaller professional networks and limited international market access. Connecting financing with procurement opportunities and international buyer discovery would create a much stronger economic model. A future BRICS framework that deliberately integrates women-led businesses into global supply chains could bring entrepreneurship and inclusion together. 9. Cross-Border Payments Will Be One of the Most Closely Watched Financial Subjects Every international MSME eventually confronts the same question: how easily can money move across borders? Cross-border payments remain costly and relatively complex for many smaller businesses, particularly where currency conversion, correspondent banking, compliance and settlement are involved. BRICS has previously instructed finance ministers and central-bank governors to continue work on the BRICS Cross-Border Payments Initiative , including exploring greater interoperability between payment systems. The previously agreed objective has been to explore faster, lower-cost, accessible, efficient, transparent and secure cross-border payments capable of facilitating trade and investment. It is important, however, to distinguish payment interoperability from frequently discussed speculation about a single “BRICS currency.” The immediate commercial priority is more practical: making cross-border transactions easier. India's own expertise in digital public infrastructure and large-scale digital payments makes the country particularly relevant to this discussion. For MSMEs, the benefits of simpler settlements could include reduced transaction costs, better cash-flow visibility and easier participation in international e-commerce. Progress in New Delhi will therefore be worth watching closely. 10. New Development Bank Could Become a Larger Engine of Global South Investment The New Development Bank , established by BRICS, remains one of the grouping's most tangible financial institutions. The bank was designed to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable-development projects across emerging and developing economies. Under India's 2026 Chairship, the role of the NDB in attracting private investment has received particular attention. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman addressed a BRICS seminar in Jaipur in August on the role of the New Development Bank in mobilising private capital in member countries , emphasising the common financing challenges facing BRICS economies. The larger opportunity is to use development-bank financing as a catalyst rather than relying entirely on public money. If NDB financing, guarantees and private institutional capital can be combined effectively, sectors including transport, renewable energy, urban development, logistics, digital infrastructure and climate-resilient infrastructure could benefit. Previous BRICS work also initiated a Multilateral Guarantees concept aimed at reducing investment risk and improving the bankability of infrastructure and sustainable-development projects, with progress expected to be reported towards the 2026 summit. Any concrete New Delhi outcome on guarantees would therefore deserve close scrutiny from investors. 11. Startups and Innovation Could Become a New BRICS Economic Bridge India is also trying to bring entrepreneurship into the centre of industrial cooperation. At the 10th BRICS Industry Ministers' Meeting, India proposed a BRICS Incubator Network and a BRICS Startup Innovation Fund to strengthen innovation-led growth. The possibilities are considerable. India has one of the world's largest startup ecosystems. China has massive technology and manufacturing capacity. The UAE and Saudi Arabia have rapidly expanding investment ecosystems. Brazil has a major Latin American innovation market. Indonesia offers access to Southeast Asia, while African BRICS members represent emerging demographic and consumer opportunities. Connecting these ecosystems could potentially create cross-border acceleration programmes, venture-capital networks, startup exchanges, technology pilots and joint innovation challenges. Sectors likely to benefit include fintech, healthtech, agritech, AI, clean technology, logistics, manufacturing technology, mobility and digital commerce. The key test will again be implementation. A startup fund matters only if entrepreneurs can access it. An incubator network matters only if startups can actually enter overseas markets. The summit offers political leadership an opportunity to turn the proposal into an actionable programme. 12. Digital Public Infrastructure and AI Could Become Major Areas of BRICS Collaboration Digital cooperation has emerged as one of the strongest tracks under India's Chairship. At meetings of BRICS communications ministers and ICT officials in Pune, discussions covered resilient digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, digital skills, startups, future networks, Digital Public Infrastructure and inclusive digital transformation . This is an area where India has significant international credibility. Population-scale digital infrastructure can reduce the cost of identity verification, payments, welfare delivery and digital financial services. If elements of this experience can be adapted voluntarily by emerging economies, the impact could extend from governments to small businesses. BRICS discussions have also included AI, next-generation communication networks and Industry 4.0. But the next generation of digital cooperation must also deal with data protection, cybersecurity, sovereignty, trust, AI safety and interoperability. Technology could consequently become both one of BRICS' biggest areas of opportunity and one of its most complex negotiating spaces. 13. Energy Security, Smart Grids and Storage Could Create Major Industrial Opportunities BRICS economies include some of the world's largest energy producers as well as some of its largest energy consumers. Energy cooperation therefore possesses enormous strategic importance. India hosted the 11th BRICS Energy Ministers' Meeting in Gurugram in June under the theme “Energy for All.” A major outcome was the establishment of the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage , together with guiding principles on smart grids and energy storage. Work has also progressed around hydrogen value chains. These developments have direct industrial implications. Rapid renewable-energy deployment requires storage technologies, grid modernisation, power electronics, advanced materials, software, smart metering and specialised engineering. That means the BRICS energy transition could generate substantial opportunities for manufacturers and technology-oriented MSMEs. India's competitive strength in renewable-energy deployment, engineering and digital technologies gives domestic businesses an opportunity to participate in these emerging value chains. The opportunity should not be viewed purely through climate policy. Energy transformation is becoming an industrial-development strategy. 14. Common Standards Could Quietly Become One of BRICS' Biggest Trade Enablers One of the least glamorous but potentially most powerful developments under India's BRICS Chairship involves standards. Representatives of national standardisation institutions met in Bengaluru in July to strengthen cooperation on standardisation and quality infrastructure across BRICS. The discussions also extended into emerging areas including artificial-intelligence standards . Why does this matter for MSMEs? Because technical standards can determine whether a product can enter another country's market. Different certification requirements, testing systems, documentation and product specifications can create major costs for smaller exporters. Greater regulatory understanding and mutual recognition — where appropriate — could reduce these barriers. Future cooperation in standards could be especially important for electronics, machinery, renewable-energy equipment, automotive components, food products, pharmaceuticals, AI solutions and digital technologies. Standardisation may therefore prove just as important for expanding BRICS trade as tariffs. 15. Geopolitics Will Test Whether BRICS Can Remain Economically Pragmatic Despite the ambitious economic programme, the New Delhi summit cannot be separated from the global geopolitical environment. BRICS includes countries with significantly different relationships with the United States, Europe and each other. Russia and Iran face Western sanctions. China and the United States remain strategic competitors. India simultaneously participates in BRICS, the G20 and the Quad and maintains deep economic relationships with Western markets. Meanwhile, conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region continue to affect energy markets, maritime routes and global supply chains. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed these issues during their August 31 meeting in Bishkek, where Modi reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy remain the way forward in resolving conflicts. Modi also said he looked forward to welcoming Putin to India for the September 12–13 BRICS Summit. India's diplomatic challenge is therefore considerable. New Delhi will need to encourage consensus among countries whose strategic interests do not always align. But this diversity could also be BRICS' strength. If the grouping can demonstrate that countries with different political alignments can cooperate pragmatically on trade, technology, healthcare, infrastructure, finance and development, it may offer a different model of multilateralism. SMEStreet Analysis: The Real BRICS Opportunity is B2B, Not Merely G2G The next stage of BRICS should arguably be measured in business-to-business connectivity . Government declarations create frameworks, but entrepreneurs create trade. If BRICS is to become meaningful for an Indian MSME operating from Surat, Coimbatore, Noida, Pune, Ludhiana, Rajkot, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Indore or a Tier-2 or Tier-3 industrial cluster, cooperation ultimately needs to translate into tangible outcomes. An exporter should be able to identify a buyer. A manufacturer should be able to identify a technology partner. A startup should be able to access an investor. An MSME should be able to finance an export invoice. A logistics company should be able to understand cross-border opportunities. A woman entrepreneur should be able to participate in BRICS buyer-seller meetings. A fintech company should be able to develop solutions around cross-border commerce. That is where BRICS can shift from diplomacy to economic participation. The USD 1.17 Trillion Question The most powerful number surrounding the summit may not be the number of leaders attending. It may be USD 1.17 trillion — the level intra-BRICS merchandise trade had reached by 2024 . If trade has already reached that level despite differences in languages, financial systems, trade regulations, geography and political priorities, stronger institutional connectivity could unlock significantly greater economic activity. But the objective should not simply be higher aggregate trade. India has specifically emphasised the importance of balanced trade . For Indian MSMEs, that means increasing India's export participation in the expanded BRICS market rather than merely increasing imports. This requires sector-specific export strategies, stronger trade promotion, easier certification, financing, digital buyer discovery and logistics intelligence. From BRICS Expansion to BRICS Execution The previous few years transformed the scale of BRICS. The next few years must determine its effectiveness. India has spent its 2026 Chairship building mechanisms across trade, MSMEs, industry, energy, science, technology, communications, women entrepreneurship, education, environment and finance. The New Delhi summit is where many of those individual tracks come together politically. The leadership challenge is therefore to convert ministerial outcomes into an integrated economic roadmap. The proposed Strategy for BRICS Economic Partnership 2030 , progress on which was welcomed by trade ministers in Jaipur, could become particularly important in providing longer-term direction. What Indian MSMEs Should Watch After September 13 For businesses, the most important developments may actually come after the summit. Entrepreneurs should watch whether mechanisms announced during India's Chairship translate into accessible programmes around MSME finance, invoice discounting, buyer-seller connections, startup cooperation, women entrepreneurship, digital trade, energy technology and development finance. Industry associations can also play an important intermediary role. Rather than viewing BRICS as something limited to governments and diplomatic institutions, Indian chambers and MSME associations should begin building relationships with counterpart organisations across Brazil, Russia, China, South Africa, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and Indonesia. India's Tier-2 and Tier-3 industrial ecosystems could become important participants in this process. New Delhi Could Re-Define BRICS as BRICS 2.0 The September 12–13, 2026 summit comes at an important moment. BRICS has expanded. Its economic scale has expanded. Its geographic footprint has expanded. Now its expectations have expanded as well. The New Delhi summit will therefore be judged by whether BRICS can transform its collective economic weight into practical institutions and opportunities. For India, this is an opportunity to influence what might be described as BRICS 2.0 — a more economically connected, technology-enabled and development-focused coalition of emerging markets . And for India's MSMEs, exporters and startups, the significance could be substantial. The most important outcome of the New Delhi summit would not necessarily be the creation of another grand geopolitical concept. It would be the emergence of mechanisms that make it easier for a small Indian company to finance, sell, innovate, collaborate and grow across some of the world's most important emerging markets . That could ultimately determine whether the expanded BRICS becomes merely a bigger geopolitical grouping — or evolves into one of the world's most consequential platforms for Global South economic cooperation. SMEStreet Perspective BRICS possesses enormous economic scale, but economic scale becomes meaningful only when entrepreneurs can access it. India's greatest contribution during its 2026 Chairship could therefore be to move the conversation from government-to-government cooperation towards government-to-business and business-to-business opportunities. The New Delhi Summit should be viewed as the beginning of that process rather than its conclusion. About The Author Dr Faiz Askari is the Founder and Editor of SMEStreet.in, a leading digital platform focused on MSMEs, entrepreneurship, business growth, policy, technology and global opportunities. With extensive experience in business journalism, industry engagement and strategic communications, he has worked closely with entrepreneurs, policymakers, corporate leaders and international institutions to highlight emerging opportunities for the MSME sector. Through SMEStreet and various industry-focused initiatives, Dr Faiz Askari continues to promote stronger market access, knowledge sharing, global partnerships and growth opportunities for Indian entrepreneurs and small businesses.
